info.desc: "Elephant" is the fourth album by the American alternative rock band The White Stripes. Released on April 1, 2003 on V2 Records, the album marks the band's major label debut. Despite this change, Heather Phares of Allmusic believed the album "sounds even more pissed-off, paranoid, and stunning than its predecessor…Darker and more difficult than White Blood Cells." The record garnered much critical acclaim upon its release, and went on to win a Grammy for Best Alternative Music Album in 2004. Elephant" is a strong, deep album showcasing Jack White at the top of his game. He rocks every guitar style .

podcast.body: In late 2001, The White Stripes recorded this album at Toe Rag Studios in London, specifically choosing the studio for its ancient eight-track recorder, analog tape, and analog console to achieve an old-school AAA (Analog recording, Analog mixing, Analog mastering) sound. Vinyl versions of this album are believed to be fully analog. "In late 2001, the white stripes book time at a studio in London called Toe Rage and the attraction was the studio's ancient eight track recorder."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Much of this album was recorded at Toe Rag, a primitive analog studio in London, England, known for its vintage gear. Jack White sought the specific sounds that only such analog equipment could provide for the album. "the White Stripes recorded much of their elephant album at a primitive analog studio in London, England called Toe Rag."

podcast.body: Released in 2003 under UB2 Records, this became the band's most celebrated album to date and definitively established them as one of the biggest rock bands of their time. A significant part of its success was attributed to the lead single "Seven Nation Army," which became an integral part of popular culture. "lanzaron el fan, su disco más celebrado hasta la fecha, y que los acabó de confirmar como una de las bandas de rock, más grandes del momento."

srcs.episode: Por qué White Stripes desaparecieron en su mejor momento?

podcast.body: Released on April 1, 2003, this album marked a breakthrough for the band, arriving "right on schedule" according to the 13-year rock cycle theory. Its sound was described as "ragged and dirty and raw and analog," a refreshing contrast to overproduced pop. "From a record called Elephants released on April 1st of 2003, those of the white stripes with seven nation army."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.body: Their fourth album, released in 2004, initially had a slow start but eventually became a monumental success, recognized as one of the most significant albums of the era. It is considered to have produced potentially the single most played indie rock song of the 2000s. "Then came a fourth album. It was called Elephant. And after a slow start, it became the monster that we're still talking about today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This album featured the single "Seven Nation Army," released a year after its iconic riff was first conceived. The song's completion and inclusion on "Elephant" propelled it to become one of the band's most popular and critically acclaimed tracks. "The song was completed, added to the elephant album, and released as a single."
